title: Lubricating the Mind and Body Before Performance
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece makes the case for deliberate warmup routines before high-stakes performance, whether physical, mental, or both. It uses the example of 80-year-old musician Steve Miller, who runs a detailed warmup of vocal, movement, and instrumental preparation before every concert on tour, to show how top performers of any age invest in preparation. The author connects this to leadership by arguing that intellectual tasks benefit just as much from priming routines like stretching, walking, or brain puzzles. The core message is that consistent, designed warmup routines -- not raw talent alone -- are what let performers show up at their best every time.
points: Physical warmup routines like stretching and walking also prime the brain for intellectual tasks.
Musician Steve Miller, at 80, runs a detailed multi-part warmup routine before every concert on tour.
Warmup and rehearsal needs increase with age, but the principle applies at any age.
Designed warmup routines, not raw talent, are what let performers consistently show up at their best.
quotes: Before every show, Miller does a 30-minute vocal warm-up while walking on a steeply-inclined treadmill.
The minute I open my mouth, I want to sing any song as good as you ever heard it.
Without a consistent warmup routine to lubricate the mind and body and to boost self-confidence, even talented and highly polished professionals will find it hard to be at their best every time.
The essential power of warming up is well-known and religiously applied by high performers in nearly every endeavor.
Even intellectual tasks benefit from physical warmup routines, such as stretching and a brisk walk to get the blood flowing and to increase the oxygen supply to the brain.
Top performers believe in lubricating the mind and body before they perform.
Some turn to reading, solving brain puzzles, or drawing as ways to prime the mind and get it ready to perform.
Almost everyone rehearses some of the same actions the performance requires, sometimes in slow-motion or faster motion to get the cobwebs out or to focus on deliberate actions.
